implementation_notes: Core Ruby has threads and Thread::Queue but no futures, so the de-facto library supplies the aggregation: Concurrent::Promises.future { ask(r) } fans the calls out on the global IO executor, Promises.zip(*promises) is the wait-for-all gather (documented as resolving the enumerable and combining the results) and Promises.any is the first-success policy. Each promise exposes value(timeout), so the deadline is enforced at the merge point, where a nil return means 'not settled in time' - the promise itself keeps running. This is the default realization for Ruby applications; the dependency-free Thread and Queue form is the second variant.
code_sketch:
promises = recipients.map { |r| Concurrent::Promises.future { ask(r) } }
zip = Concurrent::Promises.zip(*promises)
offers = zip.value(budget)                 # nil on timeout: merge what is available
return pick_best([]) if offers.nil?        # explicit deadline branch
pick_best(offers.compact)
pitfalls: value(timeout) returns nil both on timeout and for a legitimately nil result: check state (fulfilled?/rejected?) before deciding what the merge saw.
Timed-out promises are not cancelled - the futures keep running and their results are discarded only by you; long fan-outs must bound the executor or the application's threads.
The GIL makes these threads useful for blocking I/O only; CPU-bound recipients need processes, and a large fan-out starves the shared executor.

variants.name: Core Thread + Thread::Queue#pop(timeout:) gather
variants.idiom_name: Thread per recipient pushing tagged replies into a Thread::Queue drained with pop(timeout:)
variants.implementation_notes: The dependency-free realization uses only core classes: one Thread per recipient pushes a tagged reply into a Thread::Queue, and the gather pops with an explicit timeout (Ruby 3.2 documents Queue#pop(non_block, timeout:)), counting replies until all arrived or the remaining budget reached zero. The queue is the only shared structure, so no mutex is needed, and per-recipient failures are carried in the message rather than raised in the main thread (Thread#join would re-raise the first failure and abort the merge). Prefer this form in libraries that must not depend on concurrent-ruby, or when the fan-out is small and bounded.
variants.code_sketch:
replies = Thread::Queue.new
recipients.each_with_index { |r, i| Thread.new { replies << [i, safe_ask(r)] } }
offers = []
deadline = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) + budget
while offers.size < recipients.size
  left = deadline - Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
  break if left <= 0
  reply = replies.pop(timeout: left) or break
  offers << reply[1] if reply[1]
end
pitfalls: Threads abandoned by the deadline keep running and push into a queue nobody reads: their sockets stay open; kill them explicitly or bound the work inside safe_ask.
Thread#report_on_exception is enabled by default, so a worker's exception prints to stderr even when the gather handled the failure deliberately.
Queue#pop(timeout:) returns nil on timeout, which is indistinguishable from a nil payload unless the protocol wraps every reply in a tagged tuple.
